title: Indian-Led Team Finds UBC 63 Is Two Star Clusters After a Close Flyby
excerpt: Gaia data show the cluster catalogued as one system is a 21-million-year-old cluster and a 562-million-year-old cluster that passed within 23 light-years about 6 million years ago.
body:
• UBC 63, an open cluster about 4,892 light-years away previously catalogued as a single cluster, is actually two clusters — UBC 63A and UBC 63B — a team led by Gauhati University and Indian Institute of Astrophysics researchers has found.
  • UBC 63A is about 21 million years old with 98 members; UBC 63B is about 562 million years old with 148 members — too different in age to have formed together.
  • Simulations put the pair within about 7 parsecs of each other roughly 6 million years ago; they are now about 26 parsecs apart and gravitationally unbound.
  • The study, using ESA Gaia DR3 data, was published in The Astronomical Journal.

What catalogues listed as one star cluster is two. UBC 63, a poorly populated galactic open cluster about 4,892 light-years from Earth, consists of two distinct clusters that passed remarkably close to each other about 6 million years ago, according to a study led by astronomers at Gauhati University and the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) and published in The Astronomical Journal.

The team set out to study star formation dynamics within UBC 63 using data from the European Space Agency's Gaia mission. Instead, the brightness and colours of the member stars formed two distinct sequences in the colour-magnitude diagram — the chart astronomers use to read a cluster's evolutionary stage — suggesting two separate stellar systems rather than one, the Department of Science and Technology (DST) account of the study said.

Two populations, two ages

A detailed analysis of stellar motions and other properties, using machine learning techniques and dynamical simulations on high-performance computing, confirmed two populations, now designated UBC 63A and UBC 63B. The published paper reports UBC 63A with 98 members and an age of 21 million years, give or take 4 million, and UBC 63B with 148 members and an age of about 562 million years, give or take 43 million.

That age gap is the core of the finding. Stars in a single open cluster form from the same reservoir of gas and dust at roughly the same time. A 21-million-year-old population and a 562-million-year-old population cannot be one formation event — they are two clusters that happen to occupy nearby space.

A close flyby, caught afterwards

Simulating the pair's motions through the Milky Way, the researchers reconstructed how they came to be neighbours. When the younger cluster formed, the two systems were about 60 parsecs apart, roughly 196 light-years. About 6 million years ago they came within about 7 parsecs of each other, roughly 23 light-years. Today they are about 26 parsecs apart, roughly 85 light-years.

Their motion shows they are not gravitationally bound. The paper reports a present-day relative velocity of about 3.60 kilometres per second against an escape velocity of about 0.51 kilometres per second for the system — the pair is moving too fast relative to each other to stay together. Orbital integrations and N-body simulations in the paper predict the separation will grow rapidly, to roughly 491 parsecs within about 100 million years.

Encounters between star clusters are relatively uncommon, and catching one soon after closest approach is rarer still. That timing is what makes UBC 63 useful: its structure and motion still carry the imprint of the encounter, offering a direct case for studying how gravitational interactions reshape clusters over time.

Who did the work

The research was carried out by Samrat Biswas, an INSPIRE Senior Research Fellow at Gauhati University; Biman J. Medhi of Gauhati University; Sergio Messina of the INAF Catania Astrophysical Observatory; Zhanpeng Zhu of Shanghai Normal University; Songmei Qin of the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory; Sukanta Deb of Cotton University; A. H. Sheikh, also an INSPIRE Senior Research Fellow at Gauhati University; H. S. Das of Assam University; Motohide Tamura of the University of Tokyo; and Maheswar Gopinathan and Ram Sagar of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, according to the DST account and the paper.

IIA is a DST autonomous institution. The study used Gaia Data Release 3, the ESA mission's set of exceptionally precise measurements of the positions and motions of stars across the Milky Way.

Why it matters beyond one cluster

The result is also a caution for cluster catalogues. UBC 63 had remained largely overlooked, with only preliminary estimates that presumed it was a single cluster. Viewed only in projection on the sky, the two populations blended into one entry. Gaia's astrometry — positions, parallax and proper motions together — separated them.

For Indian astronomy groups working with public survey data, the paper is a concrete example of the model: no new telescope time, but precise European survey data, machine-learning decomposition and simulation capacity applied from Guwahati and Bengaluru to revise a Galactic catalogue entry. Other sparse, poorly studied clusters in the catalogues may be hiding the same kind of double identity.
